location.value: Central Europe: modern Germany plus Alsace-Lorraine and large areas now in Poland, ruled from Berlin. Colonies in Africa and the Pacific.

terrain.value: The North European Plain, the Rhine and Ruhr industrial regions, and the Baltic and North Sea coasts.
terrain.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

resources.value: Coal (Ruhr, Silesia) and iron ore (Lorraine), which powered heavy industry.
resources.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

disasters.value: The Allied naval blockade in the First World War caused severe food shortages (the “turnip winter” of 1916–17).
disasters.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

urbanisation.value: Rapid urbanisation and industrial cities. Berlin grew into a city of about 2 million people.
urbanisation.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

disease.value: Death rates fell with modern sanitation and the work of Robert Koch, who discovered the tuberculosis and cholera bacteria.
disease.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

migration.value: Large emigration to the Americas until the 1890s, and Polish workers moving to the Ruhr.
migration.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

economicBase.value: Heavy industry (steel, Krupp), chemicals (BASF, Bayer, Hoechst) and electrical engineering. By 1913 it was the largest economy in continental Europe.

tradeRoutes.value: Railways grew from 21,000 km (1871) to 63,000 km (1913). Global exports, and a merchant fleet second only to Britain’s.

wealth.value: By 1913 it was the largest economy in continental Europe. Exact GDP figures are not given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: The gold mark (1873–1914), then the Papiermark in the war, when inflation began.

inequality.value: The Junker landed elite kept great political power, while industrial workers organised into the Social Democratic Party, which won about a third of the vote in 1912.

governmentType.value: A federal semi-constitutional monarchy of 25 states, led by Prussia. The emperor (Kaiser) appointed the chancellor. A Reichstag elected by universal male suffrage, and a Bundesrat.

keyRulers.value: Emperors Wilhelm I (1871–1888), Frederick III (1888) and Wilhelm II (1888–1918). Chancellor Otto von Bismarck (1871–1890). From 1916 Hindenburg and Ludendorff held effective power.

succession.value: Hereditary in the Hohenzollern dynasty (Kings of Prussia as German Emperors).

institutions.value: The 1871 constitution, the Civil Code (BGB, in force 1900), and the world’s first social insurance system: health (1883), accident (1884) and old-age and invalidity (1889) insurance.

stability.value: The Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church (1871–1880s), anti-socialist laws (1878–90), and the November Revolution (1918).

eliteConflict.value: Tension between the emperor, army, Junkers and Reichstag. Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890. The Daily Telegraph Affair (1908).

armyAndTech.value: A powerful army (the Prussian General Staff tradition) and a large battle fleet built under Admiral Tirpitz to challenge Britain’s navy.

majorWars.value: Founded after the Franco-Prussian War (1870–71). Colonial wars, including against the Herero and Nama (1904–08). The First World War (1914–18).

territoryChange.value: About 540,858 km² in 1910 (not counting colonies). Colonies included South West Africa, Kamerun, Togoland, German East Africa, New Guinea and Kiautschou. All were lost after 1918.

alliancesRivals.value: The Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary (1879) and the Triple Alliance with Italy (1882). Rivals: France, Russia and Britain (the Triple Entente).

inventions.value: The automobile (Benz, 1886), the diesel engine, X-rays (Röntgen, 1895), and the chemical and electrical industries.
inventions.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

scienceEducation.value: A world-leading university and research system. German researchers won about one-third of the early Nobel Prizes, e.g. Röntgen (1901), Koch (1905) and Planck (1918).

openness.value: Technologically dynamic, but politically authoritarian. Minorities (Poles, Danes) faced Germanisation policies.

languageWriting.value: German, plus Polish, Danish, French, Yiddish and other minority languages.

artsArchitecture.value: The music of Brahms and Wagner, Nietzsche’s philosophy, and Thomas Mann’s literature. Expressionist art (from 1905).
artsArchitecture.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

socialStructure.value: Aristocracy (Junkers), the industrial and professional middle class, a large working class, and peasants. Antisemitism was widespread.

sharedIdentity.value: A new German national identity under Prussian leadership, with strong militarism and loyalty to the Kaiser.
sharedIdentity.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

neighbours.value: France, Austria-Hungary, Russia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and Switzerland.

ideasReligions.value: A leading centre of science, socialism (Marx, the SPD) and philosophy, and a model for social insurance worldwide.
ideasReligions.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

colonisation.value: A late colonial power. Its forces carried out the Herero and Nama genocide (1904–1908), often described as the first genocide of the 20th century: an estimated 65,000 Herero (about 80%) and 10,000 Nama (about 50%) died.

riseSignals.value: Prussian victories (1864, 1866, 1870–71), Bismarck’s diplomacy, rapid industrialisation, and scientific and educational excellence.

declineSignals.value: Wilhelm II’s aggressive “Weltpolitik” and naval race, diplomatic isolation, the blank cheque in the July Crisis (1914), the Allied blockade and unrestricted submarine warfare. Germany’s share of responsibility for the war is debated.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: German Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026); Clark, The Sleepwalkers (2012)

outcome.value: Collapse in defeat. The November Revolution forced Wilhelm II to abdicate on 9 November 1918, and the Weimar Republic replaced the empire.

sources.value: Government records, censuses, Reichstag debates, and diplomatic archives. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (only the opening part was read word for word). See also Evans (2016) and Clark (2012).

overallCertainty.value: High for statistics and events. The causes of the First World War and how to characterise the 1916–18 military leadership are debated.
